doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Fred Astaire's plunger choreography and the plunger method book
summary: Astaire choreographs Grey's plunger fills; the studio session goes badly because the playing cannot be notated, leading to Grey's plunger method book.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: They couldn’t notate the use of the color on the plunger?

That’s the reason I have a book out now, a method of the plunger for trumpets and trombones. That’s the reason I have this. Because now I get in the studio and I can’t play what they have written down here for me. And here all this money is going out the window. And I’m looking at Fred Astaire, we’ll go a few bars and they had to cut because I had messed up, because I wasn’t getting exactly what was the way it was designed for him to do for he and Barrie Chase. And he’d go down on his knees and wheel around and now this is when he was beginning to get older, see and I’m looking at

this until I finally said, and then Count Basie, he never comes out of the booth, now he comes around to me and he says, “what’s wrong, Fab?” And I say, “oh, Chief,” I said, “I can’t read this because the positions that I played with my plunger on that date I can’t get with, and it’s not written like I played it, and so I don’t know what to do.” And they were getting very worried, because here we had went into the studio like 8:00 that morning and here it is going on 11:30 and we hadn’t accomplished the first number. Now I had gotten upset and nervous and everything, and then I finally said — and you know I had a J&B’s last night, I mean when we did this recording, and everything, and I said you know, and here I’m out here and haven’t had nothing, and now Marshall Royal is laughing at me, because he’s saying that, “oh, we’re going to make a whole lot of money today because the time is running on.” And then to see Fred Astaire doing like he was there, and I’m not getting his steps in right with the plunger. That became, oh, I was so embarrassed, I was so ashamed of myself, and here the engineers and everybody’s making all this money and here Al Grey is messing it up, and was messing it up. Until finally they said, “well I’ll tell you what, we’re going to take off right now, and the band can go to lunch.” Now they’re supposed to get off at 12:00, but they cut right there, because Fred Astaire was getting pretty tired. So what happened, I said, “well let me hear the record.” And I got a piece of paper, and went in the studio, while they went out and had their lunch and everything, because, now I had become a nervous wreck. It really, in fact, that’s the worst thing in my history to this day, to ever happen to me in this business. Still the worst thing that ever happened. So now they’re out for lunch, now they got from 11:30 until 1:00, they got to have an extra half hour. And so now I’m so worried and everything, and I got a paper and started listening to this record, what I played, and I was working, and ... oh you did that, oh you did this, you closed it up here, and I started making these markings. So this is where I come up with my book. We went back and they sent out and got this bottle of booze for me, and the first one I was so nervous because I was just shaking, it’s true, you know? And so I said “give me a triple.” And I downed it and boom, I downed it and I looked over my notes again, and, thank God, the very first take we went back and it just came off just like that. And what a — and so I says, “Marsh” we called him, Marshall Royal, “you’re not going to make no more money off of me today.” And then they went on with the rest of the things that Joe had to do that day, and it came up for an Emmy and I received a gold watch from Fred Astaire.

You know that is another thought process that I want to pursue just on the side some more. And that is, even though they were trying to work from a solo that you had already played, when they went back and put it into literate culture, and put it on paper, it was hard for you to create it, re-create it. Am I correct?
Correct. Why? Because they didn’t write it like I played it, you see. See they did not write it like, and anyone in school that’s studying music today, remember that.
